He did not read it at once. He held it the way he had held the envelope, as though weight might tell him something, and then he laid it flat on the table and smoothed it with the side of his hand.

The writing had gone shaky at the ends of the lines. He knew the hand. He had seen it on feed bills and fence agreements and once, a long time ago, on the back of a photograph neither of them had wanted to keep.

"You want me to step out," she said.

"No."

He read it. It did not take long. There were not many words in it and most of them were plain, the kind a man uses when he has stopped caring how he sounds. When he finished he read it again, slower, and the second time he found the place where his brother had crossed something out and written over it, and he stopped there and did not go on for a while.

The tea cooled in front of her. The fire ticked. Outside, the wind came round the corner of the house and worried at the loose board he had also been meaning to fix.

"Well," he said finally.

"Well."

He folded the sheet along its creases and set it down. His face had not changed much. But she had been married to a quiet man herself and she knew where to look, and she looked there, and saw that it had been enough.

"He was sorry," Aldous said, to the table.

"He said that too."

"You could have told me."

"It wasn't mine to say."

He nodded slowly, as if agreeing with something further off than her, and reached for his cup."}
